speechtext:
I should like to take a moment to point out what the government has done in recognizing the situation that prevails in western Canada. In the first place we have an increased price per bushel of twenty cents. We have the delivery quota increased by fifty million bushels, and I only hope that the volume which the government plans on shipping abroad can be maintained. We have, in addition, a guaranteed price for flax of $2.25 a bushel. I listened with a great deal of interest to the address made yesterday afternoon by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris). I think everyone recognizes that when the difficulties developed in the Pacific they threw upon us immediately the problem of producing oils to replace those formerly imported. I commend the government strongly for fixing a guaranteed price for flax, but I submit that they have not been any too generous in that regard. I know that in Manitoba flax is a very hazardous crop to grow and last year very few farmers received a yield or return that was worth while. Probably more should be done, because of the extreme importance of oils to guarantee a substantial supply of flax.

In addition, the government has put a floor price of 60 cents a bushel on barley and a floor of 45 cents a bushel on oats. The government also took steps a few weeks ago to assist the sugar beet producers. Then we have the wheat reduction policy continued on a basis of $2 per acre, coupled with a continuation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Therefore on the whole the government has recognized the representations made to it and to a large degree, if not entirely, has met them.
There has been a good deal of discussion as to how much the farmer actually received for his wheat in the past year. The Searle Grain Index has been quoted on many occasions, and I should like to quote this paragraph from its last issue:
It is interesting to note that for this present crop that is now being marketed the farmers, on the average, have received or will receive the equivalent of approximately $1 a bushel for No. 1 northern Fort William. This is made up of 74 cents, the open market value of wheat, and an additional 26 cents given by the government in the form of various acreage bonuses, making $1 in all.
That is the viewpoint of an outsider with respect to what has been done, and the price this year is raised to 90 cents.
I now come to another point. Those who recall the discussion last year will remember that an attempt was made to have an assured income for the three western provinces of
S325,000,000 or thereabouts. Actually their income has turned out to be much higher, nearer to $400,000,000. The Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day intimated that on the basis of the policy for next year the return to the three western provinces would be in the neighbourhood of $475,000,000, plus about $30,000,000 in bonuses. That certainly indicates some improvement, and it is to be hoped that the results will be as he forecast, but again I point out that much depends upon the crop which will be produced, something over which nobody has any control.
A good deal has been said about parity prices. I do not propose to discuss that subject beyond pointing out two or three things. I do not think we can take the position of attempting to establish a parity price for one particular product alone applicable to a large area. In other words, if we are going to emphasize parity prices for the three western provinces, we should take in the general income of the provinces combined. Admittedly that income or estimated income is not up to so-called parity of 1926-29; nevertheless there has been a definite improvement. I have a table here showing the cash income from the sale of farm products dating back to 1926-27. That income

Wheat Board Act
in 1926-27 was $525,000,000; in 1927-28, $571,000,000; in 1928-29, $562,000,000. The estimated income for 1940-41 is $410,000,000, and if what is contemplated under the present programme is carried out and the results are as anticipated, I would think that our income for this year would be substantially improved. Undoubtedly certain areas would suffer, but here again I would point out, on the basis of these same figures, that the income back in 1931-32 was down to $167,000,000. That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the chief difficulties from which the west is suffering-the accumulation of indebtedness, the depletion of live stock, the wearing out of machinery, the lack of paint on buildings, everything connected with a depressed farm income. The correcting of that condition is one of the big problems of western Canada to-day.
If we carry through this idea of parity prices, I think we shall have to recognize at least two and possibly three circumstances connected with it. The first is that it is going to require control. We could not hope to have high wheat prices without some control, when the state is buying the wheat. At the same time, under existing conditions, and probably even under normal conditions, we would have to recognize priorities and the control effected by their use. Does not any attempt to equalize these things largely resolve itself into a question of taxation? I just point that out; I do not at the moment propose to follow it further.
An important feature of the farm situation in the coming year is the prospect of increased costs. Already labour is much scarcer and more expensive than it has been in the past two years. Added to that, the state has intervened in the matter of fuel oils; and those who are in the unfortunate position of having to buy feed grains, even for horse-power, are going to find it much more difficult to secure these essentials. Therefore, while it may appear at the moment that we are getting assistance of some value, there will be other and important offsetting features. Here may I read a letter which was recently addressed to me. If some one wants the name of the writer, I shall give it, but for the moment I wmuld prefer not to:
I saw in Friday's Free Press a report that the freezing of farm labour and a bonus was being considered. If there is any truth in this report, and you have any influence for heaven's sake get on with the freezing part of it and bonus or no, talk about that after. You know of course my own boys are all in the air force and I think I told you I had a good tractor man (medically unfit). Now he tells me that he is going out to Vancouver to take a welding course and make 200 or more dollars per month. You may of course say that this is my worry, but this is what will happen if I can not locate
another good tractor man or a good stock man. I can of course take either end myself but men in either category are just about non-existent. At present the intention is to turn off 100 to 125 hogs per year, 15 or 20 beef cattle, approx. 350 dozen eggs per month and grow 50 acres or more of sugar beets, and grow just whatever wheat the government decides is enough under present conditions. These are not visionary plans. I actually did this in 1941 and have the stock, buildings and equipment to repeat it or better in 1942. But if I lose my tractor man I will have to cut out sugar beets entirely, hogs down to one litter, cattle down to a pair of cows to supply the house and do the best I can with the grain end of it. To say we can use women or school boys is evading the question. There is no doubt we can use this kind of labour at rush times and no doubt will have to but the average woman or school boy could not take a tractor and hook on to a power drill or most other power machinery. This is a resume of my own situation but there is no doubt that it could be multiplied by many thousands throughout the country. It goes without saying that I shall do my best to carry on as I have been, both because the country needs the bacon, beef, eggs and sugar more than grain, and because I think it is the right kind of farming and something I was building up to long before the wheat situation became acute. However the chances of me being able to continue this way are anything but bright.
I point that out as indicating a situation which I fear is going to arise in connection with farm labour not only in the west but all over Canada.
Let me now refer to another matter. There are some brighter spots of which we should, I think, be reminded. We have just had a very successful campaign to raise a war loan; every part of Canada, including the west, has responded well to that appeal. I notice that the municipalities of our province find themselves in a much better position than they have been for some time. I am not saying this to indicate that there are not hardships and misfortunes in many areas in Manitoba, but I point out that there has been and still is an improvement. I hold in my hand a statement which was made by the municipal commissioner of Manitoba, and I should like to read two or three paragraphs. He says:
There has been a reduction in the unmatured capital liabilities of municipalities between 1935 and 1940 of over a million dollars.
At the end of 1935 the municipalities owed for municipal commissioners' levy, including trunk highways, $499,452 while in 1940 it was down to $365,907 and at the present time the arrears, not including the 1941 levy, are less than $200,000.
At the end of 1935 the municipalities owed the government in defaulted debentures, seed grain, fodder, and drainage liability $1,641,419, while in 1940 it had been reduced to $623,957... .
There has been a further improvement in the financial position of rural municipalities in Manitoba at the end of 1940, notwithstanding that assessments continue to decline, being

Wheat Board Act

approximately one million dollars less than in
1939	and some fourteen and a half million dollars less than in 1935.
The taxes levied have increased slightly in
1940	being one hundred thousand dollars more than in 1939, and seven hundred thousand more than in 1935.
Municipal tax arrears are lower in 1940, being forty-two thousand dollars less than in 1939, and two million, one hundred and forty-five thousand dollars less than in 1935.
During 1940 the percentage of collection of taxes, current and arrears, was 96-76 per cent of the current levy, while in 1939 it was 102-15 per cent and in 1935 it was 85-97.
During 1940, of the 169 municipalities under review, 115 operated on a cash basis, as against 109 out of 170 in 1939, and 44 out of 170 in 1935.
I think it is only fair to point out some of these things, as indicating that some improvement is being made, and that, coupled with the programme which the government has announced its intention of carrying through, and provided we get a crop, it should continue in succeeding years.
I reemphasize that the real problem of western Canada to-day turns on the matter of debt. Manitoba is not privileged by having debt adjustment legislation whereby it can adjust many of the cases which should be dealt with. That legislation has been done away with, but I hope it will be renewed, because I believe it is still necessary in many instances. If we consider most of the causes of distress and hardship we shall find that they hinge largely round two things-crop failure and accumulated indebtedness-and these problems have to be faced up to in any programme that may be undertaken.
There is only one other thought which I wish to pass on to the house at the moment. It would appear that we are going to be confronted with restricted markets, particularly for wheat and other cereal grains. Western Canada in the main is geared up to produce cereals, and wheat has proved to be the most satisfactory crop that can be produced there. Experience has been that it will stand more damage, more drought, more hardships than any other crop. If we are not going to be able to produce wheat to the extent that we have, then the situation will have to be faced. I think we should be making plans now to develop some other type of production suitable to that vast area. I do not know what it will be. It may be that we can utilize that area for growing other types of products. At any rate, I submit that there is opportunity there for a very far-reaching and fundamental type of research.
Surely that area is capable of producing something. The sooner, therefore, we try to find out what its possibilities are, the more

satisfactory will the situation become out there. Investigations have been going on in other parts of the world for the purpose of finding new uses for many agricultural products. Surely we can lend our hand in this regard, in some way or another, to see if new uses for products or new types of products cannot be developed for that vast area if it is to be taken out of wheat.

I have not the percentage before me, but I can assure my hon. friend that hog production in Saskatchewan, particularly in the last two years has gone ahead by leaps and bounds. speechtext: I have followed very closely the remarks of the ihon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Weir), and I agree with him that often when we have discussed particular cases that exist in western Canada the conclusion is drawn that we are attempting to suggest that those conditions represent the conditions which prevail in every home. I have been disturbed by references made by some members, in private conversation, to the problem that we are now discussing. It has been suggested that those of us who speak on this subject are whiners, that we
could not be satisfied under any circumstances. One hon. member said last night that he had been here a great many years and had heard the same old story over and over again and would listen no longer. I submit that my duty as a member is to sit in as one of a group of 245 charged with the responsibility of looking after a rather large family of over eleven million people. Whether we like it or not, we are living in a society and not in a jungle, and we must have controls and plans for the activities of our people, so that we can give direction along certain lines. I would remind the house that we have a problem in western Canada, and I think it is fair to say that the agricultural problems all across the country have never received the consideration that they deserve from the parliaments of the dominion. Particularly at the present time the wheat problem so far has not received in this house the consideration it should receive.
The recent victory loan campaign gives material for careful consideration. The Department of Finance, which is charged with the business of getting money to run the war and carry on the business of the country, has to get the money where the money is. I think we all agree that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is doing a very good job according to the rules laid down by the government. In planning to float this loan he asked the people in my province to raise $8,000,000 and the people in the city of Toronto to raise S180.000.000. I wish all hon. members had been in the Chateau Laurier the other day to hear the presentation made to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and members of the cabinet by the delegation from western Canada. I think all hon. members have received a copy of the brief presented, and j hope they have digested carefully the representations made. He showed that this is not a problem affecting only a few farmers in an isolated part of Canada, but one that affects the lives of hundreds of thousands of people. He referred to book II of the Sirois commission report, page 100, containing the following statement:
The people of Saskatchewan have suffered a reduction in income during the last decade which has probably been unparalleled in peace time in any other civilized country.
His worship quite rightly said that this statement covers a great deal of territory and a long period of time. He said it was significant that the mayors of the three largest cities in Saskatchewan were here supporting that delegation. They were here because they realized that if this problem was not solved, we were not going to have any cities. One hon. member with whom I discussed this question last night said it would be a good thing for all the people in Saskatchewan to leave and go somewhere else. He said he would not take $10,000 a year to live there. I asked where they should go. Starting with Toronto, I said, "How many will you take in Toronto?" He replied, "Oh, we cannot take any in Toronto; we have all we can look after; we do not want

any." We have over eight hundred thousand people in Saskatchewan, so let us start with one group of one thousand people. In the House of Commons there are 245 members. Is there one member of parliament who will say, '"All right, I will welcome a thousand people from Saskatchewan to my constituency, and they will be able to find work on the farms, in the factories or in the stores. They will find places to live, and they will become self-supporting citizens"? Where is that member? I say you cannot move a group of eight hundred thousand people simply by snapping a finger, and you cannot dismiss this problem in such an easy way.
Coming back to the delegation, let me refer to the presentation made by the reeve of a rural municipality. This man went to that community thirty years ago. He was young, and looked forward to spending the best years of his lifetime in producing necessary commodities-food for the nation. I know that this man has an enviable record in this community, and that he is one of the best citizens to be found anywhere in Canada. He said, "We owe our municipal doctor $6,000"-and I am Speaking from memory when I mention that figure. They would not have had a doctor in that community, I suppose, had it not been for the fact that the people collectively had guaranteed that the doctor would have a proper return. But can we expect a young doctor to have his salary $6 ,000 in arrears over an extended period, when there is a scarcity of doctors all across Canada? Then, he said, "We owe $6,000 to the sanatoria in our province." As hon. members understand, our provincial sanatoria are supported chiefly from municipal revenues. This particular municipality had not been able to collect its taxes, and therefore had not been able to discharge its responsibility to the sanitaria. They cannot run indefinitely on good will; they must have money to pay their staff and buy their goods. This municipality was in a position similar to that of a great many others, namely, that it was unable to meet its commitments. He said, "We owe our teachers a large sum of money, and teachers cannot live without having some financial return, no matter how much they are concerned about the educational needs of the community. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I was discussing the activities of the Department of Munitions and Supply and the various departments of national defence. I was commending those departments for carrying out the stated desire of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to use whatever money was necessary to see that Canada should make her greatest contribution.
I want to stress the fact that I am anxious that the government should avoid any policy which would lead to inflation, but I do not see how anyone can suggest that the introducing of parity prices for agricultural products could, by any stretch of the imagination, lead to inflation. Something should be said about this question of parity prices. In the United States in 1936 the soil conservation and domestic allotment act laid down these general objectives:
. . . reestablishment, at as rapid a rate as the secretary of agriculture determines to be practicable and in the general public interest, of the ratio between the purchasing power of the net income per person on farms and that of the income per person not on farms that prevailed during the five-year period August, 1909-July, 1914, inclusive.
The present secretary of agriculture of the United States spoke over the air on May 19, 1941, in connection with the regular farm and hour broadcast from Kansas city. He was

appealing to the people to give their go-ahead signal to the United States department of agriculture to carry out their plans for the coming year. I may say that on May 19 the secretary of agriculture was outlining the wheat policy for the 1942 year, while we find ourselves on March 12 debating our policy. It might be stated that the policy outlined in the United States included the fall seeding of wheat. Mr. Wickard went on to say in this broadcast:
As you all know, parity is one of the most important objectives of the national farm programmes and will continue to be a goal, just as soil conservation, for example, will continue to be a goal. We've been trying to reach that parity goal since 1933 and we've made a lot of progress.
This administration developed the parity concept and the president has worked for it all along. Had it not been for such setbacks as the supreme court decision which killed the original Triple-A, farmers probably would have had parity long ago. The president is still working for parity and in this connection, I have some grand news. I talked to the president only a few hours before I left Washington. He told me he wants the basic crops to reach parity this year. He told me also that he thinks wheat farmers, taking loans and payments into account, will get parity on this year's crop.
This news is further proof-although none is needed-that Franklin D. Roosevelt is the best friend that farmers have ever had in the White House.
The president told me that he knew farmers want fair treatment and want to be fair in return. He said he was sure they did not want loans or money paid out of the treasury to bring their prices higher than parity levels. He told me-and I use his exact words-"In this critical time, you can depend on it that farmers won': rock the boat."
It is unfortunate that Canada has no policy similar to the one in force in the United States, and I shall have more to say about this later.
To explain it simply, a parity price for farm products is a price that will enable the farmer to buy in the market an amount of goods similar to what he was able to buy during a basic period. There is always difficulty in deciding what the basic period shall be. In the United States they have taken the period 1909-14 as the base period. There would be objection to taking a similar period in Canada in view of the fact that at that time we were passing through a period of unusual expansion. Great numbers of people were coming to Canada from Europe; great numbers of United States citizens were coming north to take advantage of our cheap land. No doubt there would be objections in certain sections of the community to taking 1917-1919 as the base period. During that short time agricultural

Wheat Board Act
prices were at the highest levels in Canadian history. So our bureau of statistics has taken 1926 as the base period.
I am not prepared to admit that there ever has been a period when the farmer has had a fair share of the national income, keeping in mind his investment in land and equipment and providing a rate of wages for the farmer and his family in connection with the production of foodstuffs. For example, if you assume that the price the farmer paid in 1926 for a pair of shoes was $5, and the price he received for a bushel of wheat was $1, he was able to get a pair of shoes for five bushels of wheat. If you agree that that is a fair price for wheat and a fair price for shoes, you can start from that base. But when the farmer has to give ten bushels of wheat to buy the same pair of shoes, you must assume that there is something wrong with the price of your wheat or with the price of your shoes.
The most recent information available in Canada in connection with spreads was that placed before the Stevens' investigation, and I should like to draw attention to some of this interesting information. Those hon. members who use tobacco will be interested in knowing where their money goes when it goes up in smoke. My Scottish environment and tradition would not permit me to pay so much for so little. So I have never smoked. Those who paid twenty-five cents for a package of cigarettes in 1934 gave 11T cents to the government in the form of taxes; seven cents to the manufacturer; 3-3 cents to the retailer and 2-2 cents to the wholesaler. The farmer received 1-4 cents. When you bought a tin of peas you gave the farmer 1-2 cents; you gave the worker in the canning factory 0-75 cents and you paid 2-4 cents for the tin can which was later thrown out on the garbage heap. When you bought a tin of tomatoes you gave the farmer slightly more, 1-5 cents; you gave the worker 1-2 cents, and for the larger can you paid 3 cents.

From the report of the mass buying and price spreads investigation. When you paid 10 cents for a quart of milk you paid the farmer 4-24 cents, but you paid the dairy company enough to replace broken bottles, pay for delivery services, income tax and operating expenses and leave a net profit of one-half cent per quart. These figures show the relationship between the return received by the farmer for these commodities, and the amount which went to the other interested parties.
We find a similar story in connection with farm implements. I have in my hand a report submitted to the legislature of Saskatchewan by a special committee, upon which the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) played an important part. When the farmer paid $281 in 1936 for a binder in Regina he gave to the factory worker S22.62; he paid for raw materials $71.06; for overhead or burden, $33.93; for experimental work, $2.55, or a total cost of $130.16. The freight charges were $26.08, and the net sales realization amounted to $209.42. If you agree that the price paid by a farmer for a binder in 1913 was fair, you must conclude that the price he paid in 1940 was too high. In 1913 the farmer secured a binder for 261 bushels of wheat; in 1940 it took 637 bushels to buy the same or a similar binder. The objective of parity prices is to bring about such a price for wheat that the farmer can buy a binder in 1942 or 1941 or 1940 for the same number of bushels that it took to buy the same or a similar binder in 1926. I would ask the house, is there anything unfair about that? The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) has gone on record repeatedly that it is unreasonable to ask any manufacturer to manufacture at a loss, and I have yet to hear anyone tell of a manufacturer of machine guns or tanks or munitions or any other war equipment who is losing money. The farmers are engaged in the production of food to feed our own people and allied peoples of the world. Is it fair that those who are engaged in this necessary activity should have a return for their services that is not on a parity with the return that is going to these other groups of society?
Coming now to more controversial issues, I was disappointed with some of the statements made the other night by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). There are some things about the minister which I admire. When the government is in an awkward position there is no one on the other side who can rally the troops and make as good a case as the Minister of Agriculture. Referring the other night to the treatment we are giving our farmers he reprimanded the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Douglas) for suggesting that we should take pride in which is being done across the line and suggested that we take more pride in what is being done in Canada. He is reported at page 1210 of Hansard of March 10 as saying:
When a man cuts down his acreage to the extent that the government says he ought to, they will lend him 98 cents a bushel on his wheat. They have made loans covering considerable amounts which I have in the records here. But if he does not cut down his acreage in accordance with their request, they will lend him only 49 cents on his wheat. In other words, in the United States they lend a man twice
Wheat Board Act

as much on his wheat if he obeys the request of the government than if he does not. It is true that this has tended to set a floor under wheat of 98 cents a bushel in the United States provided the farmer does what the government asked him to do.
On the next page he says:
I should like to suggest to hon. members that I think it would be much better if we all went out and told the people what we are doing in Canada instead of telling them what they are doing in the United States. Despite what they are doing in the United States, the farmers of Canada have really been getting more for their wheat than the farmers in the Argentine and Australia. Of course, there are reasons for that.
What is the situation? I have here the report of the administrator of the agricultural adjustment administration, the AAA, in the United States for 1941. I wish the minister would use statistics instead of making general statements as he did the other night when he said that Canadian farmers are getting more for their wheat than the farmers of the Argentine and Australia. I inquired, how much more, but the minister carefully refrained from giving figures. I quote from page 20 of the report of the administrator of the AAA:
Canada alone had enough wheat to fill all available world import markets. Altogether, the world had 4 bushels of wheat for sale for every bushel the market would take. The price offered the export producers was correspondingly depressed and not far from the record-breaking low quoted on the Liverpool market just before it closed at the outbreak of war in 1939.
He is discussing the general situation. He goes on:
In Argentina, all buying and selling of wheat was taken over by the government, and producers were offered the equivalent of from 42 to 45 cents a bushel.
That is not so much less than Canadians are getting.
Australia instituted a licence system which required wheat farmers to obtain a permit to grow wheat and the government offered the producers about 51 cents a bushel on a limited production.
The United States programme, however, stands out in at least two respects. First, farmers were called upon through referendums and elections of committeemen who administer the programme, to share in the responsibility for choosing their course of action. Second, farmers cooperating in the programme received a return per bushel twice that received by producers in the other countries.
The report goes on:
This progress of the United States wheat grower was possible only because of the experience of years, experience that formed the background for the comprehensive ever-normal granary programme which has been in operation since 1939.

Then, under the heading of "Guaranteed Return" the report says:
The 1941 loan rate of 98 cents a bushel plus the conservation and parity payments of 18 cents a bushel on a farm's normal yield of wheat is providing the programme cooperator a guaranteed average return of about $1.16 per bushel.
Since its inception, the loan programme has encouraged farmers to make use of farm storage where feasible.
The other night when the minister was speaking I interrupted and asked him, as reported at page 1210 of Hansard: /
What percentage of United States farmers cooperated ?
As I heard him he replied: "Not a very large percentage," but on thinking this over apparently he considered that that would be an unfair picture of what had been done an the United States and I find that although the Hansard reporter heard the minister as I did, the daily Hansard has been changed so that it reads:
Not a large percentage cooperated by accepting loans.
I should like the house to understand the situation. In the United States it was not possible for the government to accept all the wheat that might be grown. The Minister of Agriculture, speaking of what was done in Canada, said, as reported at page 1210 of Hansard:
We said to the farmer last year that if he did not reduce his wheat acreage, he could draw 70 cents a bushel, Fort William, or approximately 50 cents a bushel at the farm on his wheat, just one cent more than he could have drawn in the United States if he had done the same thing.
We did not say any such thing to the farmer. We said: we are not going to take more than 230 million bushels, and you will have to reduce your acreage to conform to that. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) last year said something to the effect that he was "not going to pay any attention to what the government suggests because over a period of years" he had "come to the conclusion that if you do what you think is best you will be better off." I suppose he will be able to market all he produced last year. But I submit that it is not fair; those who cooperated with the government in this country expected that the government would accept 230 million bushels, and for the minister to state that the farmers were given to understand that they could sell all the wheat they produced at 70 cents a bushel is misleading. The United States is in the same predicament. They cannot accept unlimited supplies of wheat, and so they said to their farmers:

Wheat Board, Act
If you will cooperate, we will make certam proposals. It was unfair of the minister to give the impression in the house that only a very small percentage of farmers in the United States cooperated with their government. I understand that 80 per cent of the farmers there cooperated in carrying out the request of the AAA to reduce their acreage and carry out the desires of the department. They had a loan in the United States which made it possible for the farmer to realize 98 cents a bushel, and as the minister correctly said, there was a heavy penalty for those who insisted on delivering above their quota. That penalty was 49 cents a bushel, but the report makes it clear that that penalty was not with a view to collecting revenue but for the purpose of seeing that the quota was lived up to and respected.
The United States farmers have been able to get a loan of 98 cents a bushel on the farm, and naturally when they can get that, the market price has to keep in that range. A great many farmers sold their wheat at the regular price, which was around this figure. I have some of the latest available figures here in reports from Washington, which I found in the library in the minister's own department. I have already expressed that opinion with reference to the plebiscite.
But when we come to consider the agricultural policy as set out in these bills, I find it impassible to see that it will serve for the speedy prosecution of the war. I hope hon. members will realize that at a time like this there is no question, with me, of criticizing for the sake of criticism or for party advantage. In a time of national emergency no such consideration should motivate what any hon. member has to say with regard to government legislation.
The thing I particularly wish to mention is the question of wheat production by the bonusing of summer-fallow, which means, of course, the letting of land lie idle. I am forced to the conclusion that the policy of the government in bonusing summer-fallow is incorrect, because it is based upon an incorrect premise. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) has said already this session, in substance, that as far as markets go we can only look this coming year to Great Britain and, to a limited extent, a few other countries. I recall also that at the beginning of the July war loan the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), when speaking about it to groups in this city-I believe, at one of the largest theatres in Ottawa-is reported as having said that we have to regard this war as lasting possibly five or more than five years longer. That, I assume, is the premise upon which the agricultural policy

of this government is based, that we have yet before us a war of many, many years. In my view that premise is incorrect. It seems to me that it is one which is bound to result in complacency among the Canadian people, creating in them the feeling, "Oh, well, we have years and years ahead of us; we can more or less muddle along from year to year with policies which will tide us over from time to time", instead of realizing that at the present time we have come to the crucial stage of the war where we need to mobilize for speedy victory; for "if it were done when 'tis done, then t'were well it were done quickly."
There is at the present time a growing body of opinion in England, the United States and this country that if we are intent upon a very thorough prosecution of the war and a very thorough mobilization of our resources, we can create an offensive and go forward to speedy victory. I notice in our own newspapers in this city, to be exact, in the Ottawa Citizen of March 10, a report from London, England, as follows:
Soviet pressure for a second front in northern Europe which might swiftly link British, United States anil Russian troops on a solid line was increasing in London to-night with considerable Anglo-American support. The Soviet argument heard now wherever Russians, British and Americans meet, is that Hitler can be beaten by autumn provided there is bold use of his own divide and conquer strategy against him, and that once he is disposed of Japan will be considerably less formidable to the United Nations.
There was also in to-day's Journal, March 12, another report saying that in Free Europe, an international review which is published in London, the statement appears:
An allied spring offensive in the west should have a good chance for success since the forces now concentrated in the British isles presumably are stronger than those the Germans have arrayed from Norway to the Spanish frontier.
Our own Prime Minister, when speaking over the air the other night, and thanking the Canadian people for their contributions to the war loan, said:
The present is the crucial year. Germany and Japan are staking everything on 1942.
I myself am apt to believe that it is necessary for us to encourage the people of Canada to act upon that premise, that were we to concentrate to a far greater degree than we are, and to which I believe we could concentrate, victory might come far more speedily than we have been anticipating. The longer we delay; the longer we fail to take the initiative, the longer it seems to me we are going to be and the worse our position is likely to become. Our forces are becoming divided and dissipated because we are in the position of

having to defend ourselves wherever the enemy creates a new offensive. It is a wrong idea for the people of this country to believe that time is necessarily on our side. At the present time every preparation should be made for greater expediency, with a view to strengthening every nerve and every particle of our resources to bring victory this year.
One of our own men, a man in whom I believe everyone in Canada has the greatest confidence, General McNaughton, was also quoted in the Citizen of yesterday as saying that the united nations will let no opportunity slip by to take the offensive against the axis. He said:
We must resist the temptation to whitewash our forces all over the map. . . . We have never lost our intention of training our forces for attack in Europe.
Of course, we know that the Pacific situation is a ghastly one. No one is attempting to hide that fact. But I want to stress at this time that that is a part of the deliberate plan of our enemies, to distract our attention throughout the whole of the globe, if it is possible to do so. But we must never allow them for one moment to cloud or to blot out in our minds the certain knowledge that Germany is to-day the key centre of the whole world war, that in Germany the master minds and master brains who are concentrating on the world war are situated. Not only that, but in the Europe which Hitler is now dominating lies the bread-basket, the food supplies, of the whole enemy armies. Germany to-day is staking everything on 1942. Whether they and
the Japanese between them will stage new offensives in the spring is, of course, a matter of conjecture, but it is, I believe, something with which every citizen is vitally concerned and believes is likely to happen. If it is possible, we of the allies have to make 1942 the crucial year and strike before the enemy strikes, to create diversions for the enemy and scatter his troops throughout the length and breadth of the continent of Europe.
We must do what we can to encroach upon the bread-basket of the axis. In that way we shall take the offensive of 1942, and 1942 will bring victory nearer for us. If we could do that; if we could by invasion of the continent destroy some of the seeded acreage which Hitler this year is counting upon for the feeding of his armies and those vast numbers of civilians whom he has under his control, then it seems to me we would bring the conclusion of the war so much closer.

I believe in building up a reserve, the need for which may come upon us far more quickly than some of us are apt to think. Within the wheat belt in which the land can be used only for the growing of wheat I do not think we should bonus this year for summer-fallow, but the wheat farmers there should grow wheat on their land, except the amount of summer-fallow which they would normally have in the ordinary course of good farming. With regard to the marginal lands to the north of the real wheat belt, there the farmers should be encouraged to go in for raising coarse grains to provide other types of food which will also be so greater needed. I am in complete agreement with the government in regard to bonusing for coarse grains, provided, of course, there is a parity price. But the money which will, if these bills pass, go towards bonusing land for summer-fallow could be used more effectively in helping the smaller farmers to produce coarse grains by subsidizing or helping them to procure machinery for the more efficient working of those small farms. The Minister of Agriculture knows, as we all know, that during the years of drought and depression machinery on the smaller farms has run down; we have all been in the fields and seen the old binders mended with a bent nail or tied up with string and that sort of thing. The smaller farmers have not efficient machinery. Some form of government bonus by way of supplying or helping to increase the machinery at the disposal of the small farmers so that they could produce coarse grains on a more economic basis would be money well spent. I am not saying that machinery should be supplied on an individual basis. It might be better that in those northern areas groups of these small farmers should try to work on a cooperative basis, if the government would help to supply cooperative units with power machinery for the more efficient production of coarse grains.
I had hoped also that the government would have considered and given to us in greater detail some plan for increasing industry in the prairie provinces. Speaking on an earlier occasion, I mentioned the problem of wool. None of the ministers have given us much

information on that, but it does appear that in it we have an industry which, if given some encouragement by the government, might become a permanent one on the prairies and help to solve not only the problems of some of our farmers but also the problem of the unemployed in our cities.
The question of utilizing more fully this year the garden produce may seem rather a small thing, but were the government to help small cooperative canning centres for the fruits and vegetables produced on the prairies it would be a very great help, giving our prairie people an opportunity to do something more than they are at present doing. It seems an appalling thing, when you consider that to-day we are supposed to be waging a total war, to know that we still have so many unemployed. I know men can go and earn fifteen dollars a month working on the farms in northern Saskatchewan, but still there are unemployed in the cities. In the Regina Leader-Post of February 17, Mayor C. C. Williams, who, I believe, is one of those who came here on the farm delegation, is reported as stating that Regina still has one of the largest unemployment problems in the west. He said that there are on relief in Regina approximately 2,400 persons, 565 heads of families, and in addition many others whcv could be classed as unemployed, such as persons making a meagre living at part-time work. Others are getting by through exhausting the last of their small savings, and still others are able to stay off relief only by living with friends and relatives. ,
No government is waging total war unless it is making an honest attempt to find ways and means of putting to work every man and woman who is capable of working at some form of productive enterprise which will aid the efforts of this country.
With regard to prices, I feel that more must be said in detail in committee; but I am in agreement that this question of parity prices must be looked at as a war measure, if not as a permanent one. Personally I believe that it should be a permanent policy; but even as a war measure it is something that should be considered necessary, because without parity prices the farmers of this country cannot equip themselves for the production of food on an economic basis, or for the greater production of food which may be necessary as time goes on. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has spoken about morale. This session he said that there should be a place for the old, the young, the humble and the poor. One of the greatest factors in arousing a nation to a war effort is the morale of its people; that statement has

been made a dozen times in this house. In the winning of a war morale is a psychological factor, the value of which cannot be estimated in dollars and cents. It is true that the young and the old, 'the humble and the poor, must have a place in the war effort of this nation, those who look into the future with their young eyes and the old who look over the past years of their endeavour. We have these people out there on the prairies, and at the present time they do not feel that they are being given a chance to do anything toward this effort. I would say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot afford to neglect these people, for it is out of such as they that the spirit of a nation is bom and progresses.
It is the duty of a government to keep alight in the hearts of the people of Canada a flame of resolve to win this war. You cannot stop to count the cost of preserving a thing like the spirit of a nation. The policy of the government to-day in denying a parity price for wheat and other farm products I would say is a penny-wise and poundloolish policy. On the smaller farms in Saskatchewan to-day, unfortunately, you have a defeatist attitude. You may hear the people, speaking among themselves, saying to each other, "How much worse could it be under Hitler?" VTou may hear them say to each other, "We are undernourished; we are ill-clad; we lack medical care and schooling; we cannot support our churches." If you turn round and say to them, "Well, you have democracy; you can still speak; you can still send delegations to Ottawa," they will turn to you in great bitterness and say, "Yes, we have democracy. We sent our delegation to Ottawa. We asked for a loaf of bread, and the government has given us a dry crust."
This is a very difficult problem. The farmers of the prairies will go on, because they are of the breed who will not admit defeat. They will endure. They will go out into the spring rains; they will plough the fields; they will go out in the heat and the dust of summer. They will produce; but they lack the machinery; they lack the barn space; they lack the power they require on these small farms. They will do their best; but they will do it with a feeling of despair in their hearts; and when there is bitterness, despair and unhappiness, and lack of morale, these are the things which can sabotage a war effort, no matter what the government may say.
Because of these things I shall support the amendment which has been moved by the hon. [DOT]member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas). It is the job of the government to provide the sinews of war. Parity prices, such as were outlined in the brief brought here by the farmers

of Saskatchewan, are necessary to provide the sinews of war and to make it possible for our farm people to give of their best in this war effort. Food is a sinew of war. I should1 like to remind this government that if they fail any section of our Canadian people to-day, they fail the whole nation in its hour of peril, and they fail the allies to whom they have pledged a total war effort.

The then member for Assiniboia moved a resolution. It will be recalled that this was the year following the introduction of the five cent bonus on wheat. The resolution read:
Whereas the policy of extending federal assistance to western farmers on a bushel basis rather than on an acreage basis has worked out most unfairly and unjustly to the residents of those districts suffering from failure or near failure of crop,
And whereas a largely signed petition and memorandum has been presented to the government by the secretary of Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities, praying for additional legislation to partially remedy the situation that exists,
Therefore be it resolved: that, in the opinion of this house the government should give immediate consideration to a more equitable and less discriminatory solution of this problem.
In that year a man in the district which I have the honour to represent had a crop running fifty-two bushels to the acre, and he received a bonus of $2.60 per acre. Others of my neighbours had crops running forty and forty-five bushels to the acre. At that time I happened to be president of United Farmers of Manitoba, and my work took me through the southwestern part of Manitoba, where owing to drought wheat yields were as low as 8 bushels per acre.
The then hon. member for Kindersley, Mr. Carmichael, speaking in that debate said, as reported at page 292 of Hansard, of February 17, 1932:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution now before the house says that the act passed last year has worked out most unfairly and unjustly. I rather agree with that statement. In fact I heard the opinion expressed in different parts of my constituency that the act was a very good fulfilment of the Scripture: "Whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which [DOT]be seemeth to have."
He went on to say that he had received a number of resolutions from farmers' organizations and quoted this one as,typical of many:

May I pause to remind those who did not know the then hon. member for Kindersley

.	.	. after the experience of the last three

He realizes, as I fully realize, the important position the western provinces hold and the outstanding part they will play in bringing back to normal the state of Canadian economic conditions. Robert Weir and some private members of the house like Robert Gardiner, George Coote, Alfred Speakman, Ted Garland, J. L. In the budget brought down by the Prime Minister, then acting as Minister of Finance, in the session of 1931, the bonus of five cents a bushel for wheat-

-was granted to the western farmer. I am particularly interested in that bonus as I was the first member of this house to move on the floor of this chamber for such a bonus to agriculture.
What an accomplishment! I am sure there nust be thousands of monuments built on .he farms of western Canada to commemorate the action of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in proposing this great and wonderful assistance to western agriculture. He went on:
I did so on April 13, previous to the bringing-down of that budget. The exports of bacon-

We come now to 1934. It is getting better all the time! On February 8, 1934, the hon. member, speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, said, as reported at page 373 of Hansard of that year:
Let us now take the exports of wheat. During the period in which the opposition held office there was an abnormal increase in production, and exports did not keep pace with that increase. I do not know how he expected to make a handle out of that, but he does refer to it. The next place in Hansard where he refers to wheat is at page 375:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would you allow me one question? In that same speech -if you will read it-I think I suggested how to control production and delivery to the market, on the basis of so many bushels per acre on the seeded acreage, the possible exports, and everything; then, issue the quota. speechtext:
I was coming to that. I was going to give the hon. member credit for having suggested something in the nature of a quota. But the point I wish to make is that apparently all his efforts had no effect on his own government. His party was then in power. It is easy to talk when you are in opposition. I think we can excuse the hon. member for not having too much influence with the government in office to-day, but he had five years in which to work, and the price of wheat in those years, from 1931 to 1935, was, on the average, 4(R cents a bushel net to the farmer. During all that time nothing was effected but the five cents a bushel, and that lasted for just one year. A little later in the same speech the hon. member said:
But the farmers are very much concerned as to how they are to proceed to bring about the fifteen per cent reduction. I am farming on a considerable scale myself and I am concerned about it.
He then goes on to suggest something in the nature of a bonus, but nothing more came of it. It is merely an empty suggestion that gets nowhere.
We come now to 1935. One would have thought that at that time, obviously the last year his government was likely to be in office, something would have been done. In his first reference to wheat he complained bitterly of Hon. W. R. Motherwell. He said he thought that Mr. Motherwell had gone out and won an election in Saskatchewan on dollar wheat, "Vote for Motherwell and dollar wheat". He complained a second time that the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) won an election by telling the people that dollar wheat would provide a surplus for a rainy day.

speechtext: Did they get it?

PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: That makes the minister laugh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I mention these matters, Mr. Speaker, not particularly for the benefit of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, but to refresh our memories as to what consideration was given to wheat during those five years when the present opposition was in office and when the average price to the farmer was 40J cents a bushel. At one time wheat was selling in my own constituency for twenty-one cents a bushel. These are matters in which I think we should be interested, in the light of the attitude taken by hon. members like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in relation to the measure which is now before the house, and which I intend to support. I support it not because I think ninety cents is enough-it is not sufficient, I know, on my own farm-but in the light of conditions generally. I support heartily the continuation of the bonus principle. It is the only way to deal with that great semi-arid area of western Canada. I am grateful for what we have got; it means ninety cents plus the bonus.
I should now like to turn my attention to another quarter of the house. We have heard a good deal during the present session-and it is time someone said something in rebuttal-regarding the organized industrial workers of this country. Not long ago I visited one of our largest industrial plants, in which several thousand people work. As I walked through the plant, the first thing which impressed me was the small number of persons doing technical work. I saw very few jobs which I myself, were I twenty years younger, could not have done after two hours' training. As I walked through this steel plant, I inquired as to the class of material they were turning out, and the last question I would ask these young men I talked to was, "What do they pay you for this job?" From the first group I received the answer, "seven dollars for a day of eight hours, seven days a week;" and when I got to the other end of the line I found that the men there were getting eleven dollars a day. I began to scratch my head and wonder why in the world I was wasting my time as a member of parliament.
Within two weeks of the time I was there, the same crowd went on strike for higher pay. I was not very happy about it because I thought there was surely something wrong. So I sent to the bureau of statistics for some figures in order that I might draw a comparison between the earnings of these men and the earnings of farmers, the work being very similar. This is what I got. The average farm in Canada has a value of $7,202, equipped with live stock to the value of $746, and the average value of implements and other equipment is $893, making a total of $8,841. Then I inquired

Wheat Board Act

how many men were employed on the average farm in Canada and I was told, 1-2 on the average, with the operator, or a little more than two men on each farm in Canada. With all the bonuses added last year, the average gross earnings of our farms in Canada was SI,139. Take these same plants that I was in where men were working, without responsibility and without any investment; and they were earning just under $2,000-$1,960 a year. The question I ask myself is this: Is there growing up in this country a new racket? In days gone by, we spoke of the banking racket and there was the manufacturers' racket.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Not manufacturing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Under the shadow of protection we referred to them as racketeers.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: You were entirely wrong.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Then there was the steel racket, in connection with which great bonuses of many millions were paid out to the steel interests. Of late years, however, since this government of ours has been in power, what with taxation, the conscription of wealth idea, and so on, we do not hear more about these racketeers. The government has them pretty well cornered. I was in company with a group of industrialists a short time ago, and one smilingly said, "The day of the rich man has gone; the government has caught up with us." "Thank God," I said. But I am wondering whether there is not a new racket in Canada. We have heard a great deal from the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) with regard to Kirkland Lake. The other day I sent to the bureau of statistics for a statement of average wages-not salaries-paid to Kirkland Lake miners, and I would pause here to remind the house that the men engaged in those mines are not men who in the main have invested money in education. That may be their misfortune, but they have not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Are you saying they are stupid?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Not at all. I am not saying that. Those men are quite intelligent. But the point I am making is that they have not invested a lot of money in education, and they have no investment in any other form. Yet they get $1,745 a year, whereas the average farmer in Canada, with an investment of $8,841, with the help of a hired man, to whom he pays $477 a year-and taking the -2 extra, it brings the total farm wages up to $572-[DOT] receives for himself $567, and out of that he has to pay municipal taxes amounting to $80.40, fire insurance $18, life insurance, if he has any, $30, and has to provide general sup-

port for his family and pay doctors' bills, dentists, education and provide food and clothing and care generally for his family and take care of his buildings and machinery. All that he has to accomplish with $567, while we pay these racketeers, the workers in the large industries of the country, from $1,500 to $2,000 though they have neither investment nor responsibility.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: That is an unfair statement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Do you call the workers racketeers?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I sent to the bureau of statistics the other day to get figures for some specific plants in Canada and they telephoned saying they could not give them to me, but they did give me the average wage in all the primary steel industries of the country. There were sixty-five, and the average wage is $1,580, from the boy who sweeps the floor right up. The wage scale is $1,580. In other words, they get nearly $400 a year more than the farmer receives for an investment of nearly $9,000, and he has the help of a hired man and his family. That is what the farmer gets for the whole year. I mention these matters in order to point out that we have devoted entirely too much consideration to the people who have a guarantee in the form of a good job. What better guarantee could any man have than a job paying $2,000 or even $1,500 when he has no responsibility and no investment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Is that the enunciation of the Liberal policy?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I am speaking only for
myself.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Thank God for that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I was at Niagara Falls less than a year ago and I found there they were building the great international bridge. I inquired what wages the men were getting and I was told they were getting $1.50 an hour and working ten hours a day. That meant they were getting $15 a day. Two weeks after I was there they went on strike for $1.65 an hour and they got it. It does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, we are developing a new form of autocracy in this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any idea how many bridges per annum these men work on?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
No, I have not, and perhaps there may be something in what the hon.

Wheat Board Act
member has interjected. But the point is that there is plenty of steel work all over Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: You fellows have been bridging things so many years you do not understand any more.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
I contend', however, there is a serious disparity between the earnings of our farmers and the wages paid to organized industrial workers of the country.
I wish to thank the house for its patience with me and particularly the member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley), but I am sure he will not again tell us that he was the only champion, or at least the greatest champion, of agricultural interests from the west during those years to which he referred, because had he been the magician he would have us believe he was, surely he could have impressed his great leader; the then Minister of Agriculture from that province, the late Hon. Robert Weir, and some of the other members of the government, to do something for agriculture during those four or five terrible years.
There was a great deal in what the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) said this afternoon, that the problem of the west is the problem of the backlog of debt piled up during those years. I operate a three-quarter section farm, some of the richest perhaps in all Canada. For two years, 1931 and 1932, I had to go to other sources to obtain $1,000 to meet the bare running expenses of my farm. Why? Because I was selling wheat and other products at prices too far below the cost of production. I am not blaming the then government entirely for that; I know there was a depression, but I do criticize the complete failure of that government to do anything practical until just before their dying day to assist western agriculture. We all like the hon. member for Qu'Appelle; we like to hear him talk, but it is not very consistent for him now to accuse this government of failing western agriculture because it is not fixing the price at a dollar a bushel when he himself and his colleagues of that day left the farmers of the west for nearly five years selling their wheat at forty cents a bushel.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS

The subject of wheat, its production, and the price obtained for it, deserves the serious and closest attention of this house; for there is in fact hardly a constituency represented here which is not either directly or indirectly affected thereby. We from the province of Saskatchewan must be very careful to see that political considerations and political harangues do not prevent us from getting that equality and justice which we believe are, in the words of the Prime Minister, the rightful heritage of all. I regard with the

gravest suspicion, any attempt by any political party to use as a vehicle for attempted political success the great agricultural organizations of this country. I hope that such attempts will be resisted by these agricultural organizations, because if they are not the usefulness of those organizations will be drastically reduced.
I listened with some dismay the other day to the attack made by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) upon the wheat pool, because it seemed to me that by that attack he was opening up an issue andl focusing political attention upon a great and useful agricultural organization which is composed of men of all shades of political thought, and which should be so composed if it is to be of use to Saskatchewan and to Canada.
With respect to the Minister of Agriculture I have this to say: the minister in my opinion always knows what he is talking about. When we ask him a question he knows the answer, with very few exceptions, even if sometimes he does not give us the whole of it. He knows about wheat and wheat problems. I am going to repeat a suggestion which I made here last year and which has been made on many occasions, that is that he should be given the whole problem to handle, including the setting of the price and determining the advance and questions relating to it which are now dealt with by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon). I have the greatest respect for the Minister of Trade and Commerce both inside and outside this house. He has demonstrated his ability as a negotiator, but in my opinion he does not know a great deal about the wheat problem. That is only natural, because he has not had the background of experience which is necessary to know the problem thoroughly.
A few years ago I understand consideration was given to the question of transferring that phase of the work of the Department of Trade and Commerce, when Mr. Euler was the minister in charge, to the Department of Agriculture. At that time, according to the information I obtained in the press-because I was not a member of this house and did not have access to the exact information-the suggestion was opposed by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce. But I do believe that at this time the present minister would be very glad to be relieved of the embarrassment of looking after this particular' phase of the problem. At the same time the people of Saskatchewan, who are particularly and vitally interested, would prefer to have one figure on which to focus their attention, because, after all, as I imagine the Minister of Agriculture

remembers only too well, occasions do arise when particular problems come up in connection with the matter of wheat and the minister has sometimes said, "Well, I am the minister from Saskatchewan, it is quite true, but this matter is handled by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce." It seems to me that every one would be far better satisfied if one man had charge of it, one man who would be in a position to answer all our questions in connection with this particular subject.
I am not satisfied with 90-cent wheat, Mr Speaker, and I fail to see how any hon. member coming from an agricultural constituency of western Canada could be satisfied with it. Nevertheless it is a decided improvement. It is an improvement of 20 cents per bushel for the amount of wheat that is going to be taken, which amount, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated, is limited. Consequently there will be a decided improvement in the ability of the western wheat farmer to carry on. It is somewhat fallacious to be continually referring to 90-cent wheat. I know that most members of this house recognize the fact that actually it is not 90-cent wheat, but it seems to me that that fact should be impressed upon hon. members continually in dealing with this question, in order that they may deal with it intelligently. We know that 90-cent wheat means approximately 65 to 70 cents on the prairies. Last year when the price was 70 cents, No. 1, Fort William, it actually brought only 45 to 50 cents for No. 1 and No. 2 northern. I believe we should impress that upon our minds, for unless we do we shall not be in a position to determine exactly what it means to the western farmer and exactly what he is obtaining for his product.
To my mind a great deal of the credit for the improved situation as far as the wheat farmer is concerned must go to that great delegation of western farmers and business men who came to this city a short time ago and presented a most capable and most reasonably framed brief to the government, in which they requested an initial payment of $1 a bushel as an absolute minimum. They set the initial payment at $1, not because it was a parity price either on the basis of the 1913-14 parity or the 1926-29 parity; they did so because they recognized the fact that this country is passing through very tiying times; because they realized that we were in a life and death struggle, and because they knew the exigencies of the situation. But that initial price or advance of $1 was, I submit, the absolute minimum which, after very careful study and research, they felt was required to permit them to carry on under existing conditions. It was

not-and I want to emphasize this point-a basis for bargaining; it was a minimum. I was surprised to hear the Minister of Agriculture offer the suggestion on Tuesday evening that the delegation did not expect to get the $1 initial advance. If a situation has developed under which western members have thought it necessary to compromise there will be genuine regret amongst the members cf the delegation and the 185,000 people who signed the farm petition.

There is one point about this whole matter which I should like to emphasize because to my mind it goes to the whole root of the problem. As the Minister of Agriculture has pointed out, we require to ship to Great Britain, pork, beef, cheese, butter, eggs, wheat and many other products for the prosecution of the war. He has indicated also that in the majority

*of cases the producers of these products are dependent upon the treasury of Canada for a return for their production. With one exception, as mentioned by the minister the other night, the case of butter, a large proportion of the amount being paid to these producers is taken out of the treasury of Canada. Consequently I say to him and to the house: Is there any reason for a distinction between the amount paid to the wheat grower and the amounts paid to the producers of these other commodities? In my opinion those who put forth this argument are merely attempting to draw a red herring across the trail. There are not two schools of thought among the farmers. We want a continuation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act because we believe it is absolutely necessary in crop failure or near crop failure districts. For instance, in my own constituency last fall the price of wheat was not so important because we had had a partial crop failure. The assistance given under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was most beneficial. The two go hand in hand; they cannot be separated. Payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are made in cases where there is a crop failure or a partial crop failure, and these payments are entirely justified. In districts in which there is a crop failure or a partial crop failure the farmers are entitled to assistance because, when there were good crops generally, they did not get a reasonable price for it. In 1940 there were bumper crops in some districts, but they did not get enough from their wheat to put anything aside for the days of crop failure, and there, I submit, is the real justification for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

speechtext:
Now, Mt. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted to go on. I said that the Minister of Agriculture himself, in my opinion, was not satisfied, and that certainly the people of western Canada had good grounds for being discontented. In fact they were so discontented that 430 of them had to come here to Ottawa; they held their meeting over in the Chateau Laurier, at which meeting the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce were present, and I was there listening to the remarks. When they had concluded their presentation to the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce rose on the platform and said that the demands of that convention were just and fair. I commend him for that; I think he was sincere and honest. That is all these people are asking. I think they have every right to insist upon a square deal, and it was a square deal; the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) admitted that it was fair. I say, therefore, that they have just as much right to ask that their demands be granted as the industrialists of eastern Canada have to ask that they be allowed to make a profit above all their expenses, and a profit above five per cent.
I suggest to the minister that he will run into a lot of difficulty, and I think he could well afford to take a leaf out of the book of American history and to consider the suggestions made in regard to the AAA programme. Let him consider what was said by the representative of that organization when speaking in the Chateau Laurier. He gave us an outline of the way in which the agricultural organization was set up in the United States. He pointed out that after considerable years of experience they had found it advisable to organize their department from among the agriculturists. That is to say, the farmers had their small community organizations throughout all the counties in the United States, and these small organizations, or small committees, elected what were termed committee men. These committees represented something like 130,000 people. I am speaking from memory. From among them the government chose their advisers and that formed the basis of their department. It was on the advice of these men, actual farmers, that they drew up their agricultural policy.
I believe that if the Minister of Agriculture gave the farmers a share of responsibility in forming their own policy, there would be a great deal more satisfaction. He would do well, I suggest, to call into his department some of these people. In the department there are some fellows who do not know the first thing about agriculture. The minister should allow practical agriculturists to take part in 
drawing up the policy, because they have ability, as was demonstrated at the convention at the Chateau Laurier. There are some clever men among them and they could get together under the leadership of the Minister of Agriculture. I do not think they could pick a better man from that party, though they might get an improvement upon him outside. In their party, however, they have the best they can get, and with him as leader guiding them I am sure that better results would be obtained if he sat round a table with these men representing agriculture and in that way fixed upon the acreage reduction and the price, on a fair basis, allowing them to state how much acreage reduction there shoilld be, the amount of increased stock production, and so on. I believe he would get a far greater degree of cooperation in that way than he has so far obtained. In other words, I suggest that you have to give these men democracy in action. You have to show them that democracy is working for instead of against them. I could not do better than read what Mr. Evans said at that meeting at the Chateau Laurier on January 29, 1942:
I tell you this, in closing, only because that experience so forcibly brought home to me the strength of a fertile land tilled by free men, men willing to work for democracy because democracy is working for them.
I think the Minister of Agriculture will admit that the United States programme is better than ours.
A good deal has been said about the cost of production. I do not intend to weary the house by giving a great many figures, because, after all, it is difficult to follow these figures. I will speak more or less in the words of the Minister of Agriculture in reference to cost of production. Every member will recall,
I believe, that about a year ago the Minister of Agriculture agreed that the cost of production was ninety cents on the farm, and I think he made a conservative estimate. He just about hit it. I do not like to flatter him at all, but his judgment is good. The Minister of Agriculture agreed that ninety cents was the cost of production, and he who was in charge of agriculture must take responsibility along with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for setting the price at seventy cents.

speechtext: While the minister may be correct in saying that, it is nevertheless true that he said on that occasion as well that the farmers would lose around $100,000,000. That would be the loss to the farmers.
