subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: That was their cash loss. I do not care what you call it; it comes out of their pockets. It is all right for the minister to say now that the farmers will get a dollar a bushel. You can sit here and do all the figuring you like, but when you ask the farmer what he got for his wheat and he tells you he got forty-eight cents, it is mighty hard to convince him that he got a dollar. It is as the hon. member for Battle River said the other night. What the farmer actually received was forty-eight cents, and you cannot convince him that that is a dollar unless you are a magician.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but if I may be permitted again would point out that the other night I could have read the letters to which I referred, and there were letters from farmers stating that they did get at the farm as high as $1.40.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
That might have been an individual case, but that is certainly not the average. In some particular
instances, with other farm produce they marketed, the total return may have come up to that. I am not disputing that, but I say that that was not the average. I am saying that the farmers in most instances did not get anywhere near it. If I recall rightly, the minister said the other day that the farmers this year would not make any money. I cannot understand why it is that every other industry in Canada is not asked to carry on at a loss. Other industries are not expected to. There is only one industry, and that an industry we could not do without for one year without total failure in this war, and that industry is agriculture. Only that one industry is asked to produce at less than cost. Surely my hon. friends from eastern Canada must understand that that is not a fair proposition. You are not going to have unity when here in eastern Canada they get $1.26 for their wheat and out in the west under this new programme' they are going to get ninety cents at Fort William.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: That $1.26 is delivered: at Montreal.

speechtext: I wish hon. members would speak on their own time. The price set in eastern Canada is $1.26 a bushel.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext: At Montreal.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Yes, and
the 90 cents is at Fort William, not on the farm. Of course it may be said that this is for soft wheat. I do not care what it is for; the fact is there is discrimination there, and very unjust discrimination. Let me read what was reported in the Lethbridge Herald of March 9:
J. H. Wesson, Saskatchewan wheat pool president and chief spokesman for four hundred farm delegates which presented the petition to the federal government last month, said the farmers would insist ninety cents a bushel was not sufficient.
"We will continue to urge that the initial payment in the crop year 1942-43 be $1 a bushel, and that further payments to bring up the wheat price to a 'parity' level be made during the crop year," Mr. Wesson said.
Mr. Wesson said the farmers would be content to have the "parity" price established by the dominion bureau of statistics.
You cannot expect anything fairer than that. Why the government persist in agitating such a great number of people in that way, when they know the proposition they make is unfair, I just cannot understand, unless, of course, the Minister of Agriculture had in mind what he said the other day as reported at page 1211 of Hansard:
I would say to him that any member of this house who carries back into western Canada the government's policy in relation to wheat
Wheat Board Act

and its policy in relation to other farm products can stand before any audience and explain to the people there that this is the best that can be done under the conditions with which we are confronted in the Dominion of Canada to-day, and the best that has been done in an attempt to settle their problems at any time. We are taking every last dollar out of the treasury of Canada to deal with these problems which we feel it is safe to take at this present time.
That is an absolute contradiction of what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) have stated on different occasions. The Minister of Agriculture says we are doing everything we possibly can for the farmer in view of the fact that money is limited; that we are taking everything out of the treasury that we think we can safely take. The Minister of Finance said on more than one occasion when speaking to the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), "We are going to make financially possible anything that is physically possible. There is going to be no money restriction." The Prime Minister said-the words have been repeated so often in this house that I hardly need remind hon. members of them

"We shall issue currency and credit in times of public need." Which is right? The Minister of Agriculture says to the farmers: "I cannot do anything more for you fellows, much as I would like to, because my hands are tied, because of the financial strings that hold me back." But the Minister of Finance says: "That is not right because we are going to make financially possible anything that is physically possible." I think the western farmers have good reason to complain. I should not be surprised to see them on the train coming here again and demanding a square deal, and I believe the Minister of Agriculture would be the last man to say to them, "You are asking something unreasonable."
Let us now look at the income the farmers have. I am not going to quote figures at length, but I want to put on the record some statements from the Searle Grain company's letter. We all admit that they keep very careful watch on this critical situation. This is from No. 22 of November 19, 1941:

The figures for 1941-42 are, of course, estimated. Remember that the total revenue for 1928 was $611,780,000. That brings, generally speaking, about $45,000,000 less for 1941-42 than they received the year before. It is an estimate, but based on good sound calculation. They go on to say:
There are, in the three prairie provinces, approximately 300,000 farming families. It will be seen, therefore, that the annual average income for wheat alone for each family will be $506 from wheat, and from all other sources other than wheat $616, making the total income for the average farming family $1,122 for this year. Out of this total sum of $1,122 each farming family has to pay its living expenses for the year, and the costs of growing, harvesting and hauling to market its farm products . . .
The index includes 16 items of groceries; 36 of clothing; 28 of household equipment; 53 of farm equipment; 12 of farm machinery and two items of school and municipal taxes. These items, we find, cost farmers to-day $1,004 a year. It will be observed therefore that each prairie farming family has on the average only $118 left ($1,122 minus $1,004) with _ which to pay for all those things which farming families require, and which are not included in the 147 items in the Searle index.
Out of that total profit-if we call it a profit-of $118 from their entire return including the bonus, they have to pay the interest on mortgages and loans and for such small extra comforts as any family requires. It is amazing that the government, knowing that the farmers were producing at a loss and are compelled by quota to sell only a certain amount, did not cut down the interest on farm mortgages. Why should they not have made it possible to lower the cost of production by lowering the cost of machinery by lowering the tariff?
Before this bill passes the minister should- and I do not believe he would be condemned for it by anyone, even members of the cabinet-form an advisory council of agriculturists, the same as industry has. Industry would not think of letting a bunch of farmers come in and run their industry and set the profit they would get. They would not even allow members of parliament to set the profit. Then why should anyone object if the agriculturists come in and assist the minister to deal with problems and policies regarding their own industry? I believe the minister would be well advised to clip that sheet out of United States history. He should raise the price to $1 a bushel. Mind you, we have always advocated $1 a bushel at the local elevator. Then probably it would be advantageous to pool the freight rates, so that everyone would be treated alike. There should be no reason for the eastern farmer to complain and say, "Well, we are not getting

Wheat Acreage Reduction
as much as the west," or for the west to say, "We are not getting as much as the east." There must be some pooling arrangement as to freight rates, so that every farmer will be treated alike.
Then you must give the farmers the parity price; they have a right to ask for it. If the government does not give it to them, I hope the farmers come here again and sit right on the doorstep until they get it. Apparently that is the only way they will get anything, and I believe the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce are asking for just that sort of thing. You cannot expect people to go on fighting for democracy in this war when the very thing for which they are fighting abroad is denied them at home. I think the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce should get together and talk to these other fellows in the cabinet a little bit. Surely they will come to reason and let democracy live in Canada.
